questions: Are you aware of these mouth and tongue movements while they are happening?
Can you voluntarily stop the movements for a few seconds when asked?
Have these movements been present for more than 3 months?
Do you take or have you recently taken an antipsychotic medication such as haloperidol, risperidone, or olanzapine?
Do you take or have you recently taken metoclopramide or prochlorperazine?
Did the movements begin after starting or increasing one of these medications?
Do you have difficulty swallowing or speaking because of these movements?
Do you also have involuntary movements of your limbs or trunk?
Have you ever had a seizure or loss of awareness associated with these episodes?
Are the movements absent during sleep?
Do you wear dentures or have poorly fitting dentures?
Do the movements improve or disappear when you are chewing, speaking, or eating?
Do you have an urge or uncomfortable sensation before the movements that is relieved by making them?
Do you have stiffness, slowness, tremor, or reduced arm swing when walking?
Have you ever taken levodopa, amantadine, or another medication for Parkinson’s disease?
Do you have problems with memory, judgment, personality, or thinking?
Has anyone in your family had similar involuntary movements or a diagnosis of Huntington disease?
Do you have a history of stroke, head injury, brain infection, or other neurological disease?
Do the movements worsen with anxiety or concentration?
Do the movements stop when you are fully asleep?
Do you also have involuntary forceful blinking or spasms around either eye?
Do you have involuntary neck movements or difficulty keeping your neck still?
Do the movements mainly consist of repetitive chewing, lip-smacking, tongue protrusion, or jaw movements?
Do the movements continue while you are asleep, as observed by another person?
Have the movements gradually become more frequent or severe over time?
Do you have any difficulty controlling your jaw, tongue, or facial movements when you deliberately try to perform a precise task?
Do you have any recent dental pain, oral ulcers, or irritation inside your mouth?
Have you ever used recreational drugs, including cocaine, amphetamines, or methamphetamine?
Do you drink alcohol heavily or have you recently stopped drinking alcohol?
Does touching your face, chewing gum, or placing something in your mouth reduce the movements?
Have you ever taken antidepressants, stimulant medications, anticonvulsants, antihistamines, or other medicines for nausea or dizziness for several months or longer?
Have you ever taken an antipsychotic or anti-nausea medication in the distant past, even if you no longer take it?
Did the movements begin before or after any dental extractions or loss of most of your natural teeth?
Do you have a history of diabetes, thyroid disease, or other metabolic illness?
Have you had any involuntary movements of the face or mouth during earlier periods of your life?
Do the movements consist mainly of sustained jaw opening, jaw closing, or jaw deviation rather than rapid repetitive chewing or lip-smacking?
Do the movements become more pronounced when you speak, read aloud, or voluntarily move your tongue?
Do you have painful spasms or stiffness in the jaw or tongue?
Do you have involuntary movements of the lips or tongue while your jaw is otherwise still?
Have you ever had similar involuntary movements during a dental examination or while wearing a mouth guard?
Are the mouth and tongue movements present when your face and jaw are completely at rest?
Are the movements regular and rhythmic, occurring at a fairly constant rate?
Do the movements stop or lessen when you are asked to perform a competing movement with your hands, such as finger tapping?
Do you have a tremor of your jaw, lips, or tongue when holding them in a fixed position?
Have you had any exposure to medications for Parkinson’s disease, even briefly, including levodopa or dopamine agonists?
Did the movements begin suddenly over a period of days or weeks rather than gradually over months or years?
Do the movements vary markedly from one moment to the next or disappear for long periods while you are awake?
Can you intentionally imitate or reproduce the same mouth and tongue movements on command?
Are the movements triggered specifically by speaking, reading, or other voluntary mouth movements, but absent during quiet rest?
Do you have any abnormal involuntary movements elsewhere in the face, such as forehead wrinkling, nose movements, or facial grimacing?
Have you noticed any change in your voice, speech articulation, or ability to pronounce words?
Do you have difficulty coordinating chewing or swallowing solid food despite normal strength?
Have you had a recent major emotional stressor or traumatic event before the movements began?
orders: Bedside movement-disorder examination with observation of the mouth and tongue at rest, during spontaneous conversation, reading aloud, sustained vowel production, rapid tongue movements, chewing, and distraction; assess for task-specific dystonia, a sensory trick, distractibility, and entrainment.
served: distribution of the dystonia (focal, segmental, generalized)
